Figure 1:A relevant past can be wrong for the present.Three qualitative failures from earlier Track-B testbed rollouts
(not the main quantitative rerun), showing previous appearances,
retrieved frames, composed keyframes, and generated clips.Top:a deceased character reappears when a jacket is mentioned.Middle:a white look-alike replaces the requested orange dinghy.Bottom:retrieved frames preserve Axi’s old scarf despite a
new instruction specifying a short cape. Symbols indicate
required-entity matches (✓), misses (×\times), and
forbidden appearances (!). These examples illustrate failure
paths; they are not fixed-history causal interventions.

Figure 6:What is hard on Track-A.Continuity recall by entity type (first six columns) and LSMDC event (last four). Darker orange means higher recall on a fixed 0–1 scale. Released memories, below the horizontal line, have lower recall across displayed slices. DINO-key leads nine slices; Text-frame leads LSMDC props.

Figure 8:From S1 draft to frozen gold.In twoSpringsegments, the VLM draft describes the
action but leaves entities that are on screen unnamed, and the first draft also borrows an action from the
next segment. The frozen instruction names every present entity by its roster name, so a memory can be asked
for each of them. The footer counts the same kind of change over the whole corpus.

Figure 9:Anatomy of a Track-A film(Spring, Blender Studio, CC BY 4.0). Top: five story
segments with the instructiongng_{n}the system receives (English excerpts of the Chinese gold). Bottom, on
grey: scoring-only gold for ten of the film’s eleven entities over segments 0–39 (the rest are titles and
credits): where each entity is on screen, its state events, and the per-segment diagnostic tags. The grey
puppy leaves after segment 10 and returns in segment 15, the case shown in Fig.12.

Figure 11:Track-B judge verdicts checked against human labels on real units.Each row shows the
entity’s previous appearance in the same rollout, three frames of the generated clip, the verdict of the
pinned Qwen3-VL-32B judge, and the human label for the clip. In rows 1, 4 and 5 the judge is right about a
required entity being present or absent and about a forbidden entity being rendered; 28 of 32
judge-confirmed controls were confirmed. In rows 2 and 3 the judge reports a required entity as missing
although it is clearly rendered; such misses make up 27% of sampled required-entity failures and
concentrate at long gaps and time references, so Track-B recall there is conservative.

Figure 12:Every reference two memories hand over forSpringsegment 15.Text-frame returns 16
near-identical views of the girl in the forest and never the puppy, last seen five segments earlier.
Seg+DINO-key samples diverse views, finds the puppy on the cloud ridge (74 s), and covers all four entities,
but five of its 15 references show none of them. Letters are the automatic judge’s labels; it also tags some
misty-forest frames before 144 s as the nest, which does not change which references count as correct here.

Figure 14:Track-B rollouts on two memory probes: memory brings back a recently seen character, and
also a dead one.Rows are systems given the same prompt stream; columns show the entity’s previous
appearance and the probe segment (middle frame of each generated clip). In (a) the no-memory generator draws
a stranger for “he” while all four retrieval memories restore the ranger; in (b) no memory keeps the dead
guard out, but all four retrieval memories, MemFlow, and IAMFlow put him back at his plaque. Badges are the
automatic judge’s verdicts for that entity, and Track-B Recall and Avoid-OK pool such verdicts over all
2,824 segments; the released systems use their own generators.
